definitions.definition: When two different things have the same shape or structure, even if they are made of different stuff.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system and the actual subway tunnels have the same structure (stations and connections), even though the map is paper and the tunnels are underground.

definitions.definition: The study of heat, energy, and how they move and change in systems.
definitions.example: When you boil water, thermodynamics explains how the heat from the stove turns the water into steam.

definitions.definition: The study of sin in Christian theology.
definitions.example: Hamartiology asks questions like 'What is sin?' and 'How does sin affect people?'

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; in an isolated system, it always increases over time.
definitions.example: A messy bedroom has higher entropy than a tidy one, and without cleaning, it will only get messier.

definitions.definition: A system that does not exchange energy or matter with anything outside itself.
definitions.example: A sealed, perfectly insulated thermos of hot coffee is almost an isolated system—no heat or coffee gets in or out.

definitions.definition: In this framework, the unchanging moral reality of God that everything else can align with or fail to align with.
definitions.example: Think of it like a perfect radio signal that never changes; a radio can pick it up clearly or with static, but the signal itself stays the same.

definitions.definition: A mathematical way of saying that the coherence field (C) does not spread out or shrink; it stays constant.
definitions.example: Like a perfectly still pond with no ripples—the water level is the same everywhere.

definitions.definition: A number that measures how strongly a system connects to an external source, like grace.
definitions.example: Like the volume knob on a speaker: a high coupling coefficient means you hear the music clearly; a low one means you barely hear it.

definitions.definition: Always moving in one direction, either always increasing or always decreasing, never reversing.
definitions.example: A countdown timer monotonically decreases—it never goes up.

definitions.definition: A process that cannot go backward on its own; once it happens, you cannot undo it without outside help.
definitions.example: Burning a piece of paper is irreversible—you can't unburn it and get the paper back.

definitions.definition: Relating to the shape or structure of something, ignoring exact sizes or measurements.
definitions.example: A donut and a coffee mug are topologically the same because each has one hole, even though they look different.

definitions.definition: Relating to exact measurements, like distance, weight, or energy.
definitions.example: The metric system uses meters and kilograms to measure things precisely.

definitions.definition: A formula that connects entropy to the number of ways a system can be arranged at the microscopic level.
definitions.example: It's like counting how many different ways you can scatter LEGO bricks in a box—more ways means higher entropy.

definitions.definition: A specific, detailed arrangement of all the tiny particles in a system.
definitions.example: If you have three coins, one microstate is heads-heads-tails; another is tails-heads-heads.

definitions.definition: An idealized engine that converts heat into work with maximum possible efficiency.
definitions.example: Think of it as the perfect car engine that wastes no energy—but it's only a theoretical model.

definitions.definition: The belief that people can save themselves or become morally perfect without God's help.
definitions.example: Pelagianism is like thinking you can clean a filthy room without ever using water or a broom.

definitions.definition: The idea that sin has affected every part of a person, so no part is untouched by moral corruption.
definitions.example: It doesn't mean everyone is as evil as possible, but that every part of you—mind, heart, will—is affected by sin, like a cake that has gone bad all the way through.

definitions.definition: The process of becoming more holy or morally pure, often through God's help.
definitions.example: Like slowly cleaning a stained shirt until it becomes white again.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation—how people are saved from sin and its effects.
definitions.example: Soteriology asks questions like 'How does God save people?' and 'What is the role of faith?'

definitions.definition: The idea that a scientific theory must be able to be proven wrong by some possible observation or experiment.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' can be falsified by finding one black swan.

definitions.definition: A principle saying that erasing one bit of information in a computer always produces a tiny amount of heat.
definitions.example: Every time you delete a file on your computer, a tiny bit of heat is released, even if you can't feel it.

definitions.definition: A scientist who helped formulate the Second Law of Thermodynamics, which says entropy always increases.
definitions.example: Clausius is like the person who discovered that your messy room will never clean itself.

definitions.definition: Special variables used in this framework to represent different aspects of reality, like entropy (S) and grace (G).
definitions.example: Think of them as labeled boxes that hold different kinds of measurements for the theory.
